Even as the hyperscalers dial back buybacks to fund AI spending, BofA’s data shows Tech buybacks shooting higher.

▪️ Tech’s rolling 12-week corporate client buybacks climbed to $5.6B by the end of October from $3.2B at the start of the month, lifting it from 4th place among sectors in September to 2nd.
▪️ That puts Tech just behind Financials ($7.2B), which had led it by roughly 5x in early September, by our calculations.
▪️ Overall 4-week average buybacks swung to +84% YoY from -41% in mid-September.

Worth noting: Alphabet and Meta are classified as Communication Services and Amazon as Consumer Discretionary, so most of the hyperscaler pullback wouldn’t show up in BofA’s Tech numbers. Microsoft is the main exception. The surge looks broader-based across Tech.

Tons of US car owners owe more on their vehicles than they are worth:

29% of trade-ins for new-vehicle purchases involved negative equity in Q3 2026, near the highest proportion since Q1 2021.

At the same time, the average amount owed on underwater vehicles rose to $7,107, the 3rd-highest on record.

This is +$2,960 above the low recorded in Q4 2021 and +$1,850 above pre-pandemic levels.

Meanwhile, buyers who rolled over unpaid car debt into new loans took on an average loan balance of $57,235, up +44% from 2019.

The average annual percentage rate (APR) for these borrowers was 8.1%, pushing total interest payments over the life of their loans to $16,610, up +83% from $9,093 in 2019.

The US is in a car affordability crisis.

BREAKING: The US Social Security Trust Fund’s deficit jumped +$39 billion YoY in Fiscal Year 2026, to a record -$221 billion.

This fund finances retirement benefits and payments to eligible survivors of deceased workers.

This comes as the fund’s costs, primarily benefit payments to retirees and survivors, soared +$83 billion YoY, to $1.5 trillion, an all-time high.

At the same time, income, primarily from contributions to the Social Security system, rose +$44 billion YoY, to a record $1.3 trillion.

Since FY2022, the fund’s deficit has surged +$188 billion, or +585%.

As a result, trust fund reserves fell -$221 billion YoY in FY2026, to $2.18 trillion, the lowest since 2007, down down -$640 billion from the 2017 peak.

The financial health of Social Security is deteriorating rapidly.

Food prices are climbing again, and the money printer has nothing to do with it.

Groceries rose across almost every aisle in October, led by fresh food. The cause is upstream: diesel is up more than 60% since the Iran war began, and truck freight costs are up over 17%. Energy moves through everything that gets grown, shipped, and stocked.

This is a price shock, not inflation. An oil war spikes diesel, diesel spikes freight, freight spikes food. It clears when the barrels come back.

tweets.text:
🚨 🇺🇲 Next week, Nvidia could absolutely crush earnings expectations on Tuesday and still see its stock collapse.

📊 Wall Street expects around $109 billion in third-quarter revenue representing 90% YoY growth followed by almost $125 billion in the fourth quarter. Absolutely insane numbers but how much longer its customers can afford to keep buying its GPUs ? Nvidia has become much more than a chip supplier as it's now actively financing parts of its own ecosystem through investments, financial guarantees, and massive supply commitments. Its latest financial filings revealed approximately $530 billion in commitments and exposures of various kinds, including $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments. Nvidia helps finance companies building data centers that ultimately purchase Nvidia's own GPUs. As long as capital keeps flowing, the machine works, but if these infrastructure investments fail to generate sufficient returns, the entire system becomes much more vulnerable.

➡️ Jensen Huang's departure changes many things. We're talking about a CEO who personally controlled an extraordinary number of Nvidia's strategic, commercial, and financial decisions. Colette Kress, now serving as interim CEO, had reportedly already pushed back against some of Huang's more aggressive financing initiatives. If she decides to scale back the guarantees and investments Nvidia provides to its partners, from a growth perspective, it could create serious problems. Less financing potentially means fewer data centers getting built, which means GPU orders being pushed further into the future, and all of this is happening while financing conditions are tightening, major technology companies are borrowing heavily, and the Democrats' takeover of Congress could introduce additional obstacles for certain infrastructure projects.

⚠️ The stock has already corrected significantly and the company continues to generate extraordinary amounts of cash. A strong quarter combined with reassuring guidance could easily trigger a violent relief rally. However, if Nvidia delivers exceptional results but starts talking about delayed projects, reduced visibility into 2027–2028, or a reassessment of its financial commitments, I would take that extremely seriously. 

Next Tuesday will especially be about how long the company can sustain this kind of growth without having to help finance the demand for its own products.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/OnvN3z5RZe

tweets.text:
159 years ago today, the first stock ticker tape debuted… 

On November 15, 1867, the first stock ticker debuted in New York City, changing how quickly investors could follow the market. 

Developed by Edward Calahan, the machine transmitted stock quotes over telegraph wires and printed them on paper tape, earning its name from the ticking sound it made. 

Investors who had relied on messengers to deliver prices could now receive updates directly, making it easier to track trading beyond the exchange floor. 

It’s easy to take instant quotes for granted today, but 159 years ago, a strip of paper represented a major technological advance on Wall Street.
